title: Learn from these mistakes before building a game
author: Remarkable-Survey880
selftext:
Here are some things I’ve learned over the past few months to hopefully help you not make the same mistakes I did. 

**1. Plan out your entire game from start to finish before you ever start actually building** \- The story, gameplay, design, sound, lighting, art, etc. This will save you tremendous headache, time, and usage waste down the road. 

**2. Use prompts to your advantage**. If you tell the AI to do something, it will do it how it sees fit NOT through your own vision. Use plenty of prompts to guide your vision. For example, “The games lighting must use current industry standards and best practices achieving realistic lighting across the entire game” or “Before making any design decisions research the top games in my genre and how they work so I can apply it to my game” Obviously these can be tweaked better. 

**3. Set up a QA lane -** Setup a lane that uses a cheap model that is explicitly read only that goes through the entire game and runs a QA looking for bugs, etc. You can set this up to run on a timer. 

**4. Use outside resources -** You can find a ton of free stuff such as audio, vfx, materials, textures, animations etc. Use this to your advantage especially to free development on other things. 

**5. Know your limitations and the AI’s limitations** \- Do not expect to make a AAA game it just isn’t feasible, once you understand and accept this you can begin to work with what you can do and achieve.

comments.author: Mubeenization
comments.body: Thanks. Can you please elaborate on how to setup a QA lane please?

replies.author: Project_Asura
replies.body: Yes agreed maybe create a subagent to run autonomously double checking QA every so often

replies.author: Remarkable-Survey880
replies.body: Start a fresh session under your project using a cheaper model, for instance if you are using Claude use a Haiku or Sonnet model and give it a prompt to run a QA (quality assurance) pass every X minutes or whenever you choose, which runs a systematic test to find bugs, glitches, performance issues in the code/game itself then give it instructions to handoff its findings to another session that can fix them etc before they ever become an issue.

comments.author: meowyih
comments.body: About the first “mistake” you mentioned, all I can say is that it is just impossible, except you are copying other existing game. No matter you are a solo dev, in indie dev team or work for AAA game company, it’s just not possible to create a game plan that you can follow throughout the entire dev lifecycle without changing it.

replies.author: Remarkable-Survey880
replies.body: I get that and you’re right. My point was people like me probably jump at a good idea that pops into their head and starts running with it without planning the entire scope through and working out the kinks first and then ends up wasting time and burning usage changing a ton of stuff that could’ve been avoided to begin with.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
True. Often an idea is to general and needs to be focused. Like I want to build a shooter, but what actually goes into it. 

And people: Do the research! 
If your building something, don't think that you know everything. Like Socrates said: you know that you don't know. 

And use an engine if you want to go Steam (don't build your own). Know that only a very small part of ai games earn money on steam, not because they are ai but because they are shit. Most people don't care if ai is used. And most ai games never reach the 1000 bugs threshold.

replies.author: lucianw
replies.body:
I think you should build a really lightweight prototype of the first level. Zero graphics, just plain rectangles or whatever. Iterate on the gameplay. And continue this prototyping for something that will give a feel for how the gameplay or story develop in later levels.

If you can make this fun, only then move onto graphics and lighting.

replies.author: Entropydemic
replies.body: He wasn't saying not to change it though, he was saying that a plan makes for an ideal follow-through. You'll run into all sorts of issues through the whole process. A plan is to help sort through things when an inevitable change occurs.

comments.author: Renizance
comments.body:
I've worked at AAA game studios. No one, absolutely no one has a game figured out start to finish at the kick off of a project. That's insane.

Yah plan as much as you can but what's on paper and what's actually fun is not always aligned. You gotta be flexible and adapt.

Do look dev, have a direction, explore mechanics on paper so you don't waste tokens flipflopping to much. That's good advice. Having it all figured out step for step before hand is unrealistic and perhaps even detrimental to your game.

replies.author: Spudly42
replies.body: Yeah first step is probably to prototype your base mechanics and make sure it's actually fun.

replies.author: fattybunter
replies.body: Step 1 just make the entire game. Just do that for step 1. This was absolutely not suggested by AI

replies.author: Ok-Sea300
replies.body: AAA game studios hate this one simple prompt: "Make sweet game bro, make it so sweet and make no mistakes. Go on loop until game is sweet ass sweet sweetest one in genra bro*

replies.body:
So I tried this and Fable 5.2 just made Call of FIFA 2029 Year of the Gun Edition for me in a single prompt, this is insane. Already sold a few million copies on steam and epic store. We are cooked. 

/s

replies.author: Ok-Sea300
replies.body: You said Epic store so we know its real! ;)

replies.author: Own_Badger6076
replies.body:
The main thing I've learned from working with AI on software projects isn't to "plan it all out from start to finish" (what are you doing, plotting a novel?), but you do want to setup an organized project folder to get started with for doing all the things you might need to do during a big software development project. 

You also want to be reviewing your repo regularly and doing unit testing to ensure shit it works well and isn't becoming a giant mess.

replies.author: PostNuclearTaco
replies.body:
I plan milestones with human checks throughout and a thorough test at the end of each milestone as well as playing with all the new features to see how they feel.

First milestone was a character controller and simple gameplay mechanics. Second was adding in new mechanics and tooling for level design. Third was more mechanics plus a pass to upgrade from demo art to use the spritesheets I made. Etc.

I create a plan and work out all design decisions ahead of time then I build through them in phases. I have a document that tracks my design decisions and I have explicit instructions for the AI not to make creative decisions and to get my say on any decisions regarding creative design.

This way it keeps me adaptable if I find something that works or doesn't, keeps me organized to prevent the project from descending into slop, prevents drift, and prevents the project getting out of control due to lack of oversight.

replies.author: Remarkable_Lead_1538
replies.body: i still after 5 months still making big changes

comments.author: thepandapuncher
comments.body:
Agree with it all. First few games I made were me jumping at an idea and quickly losing track. Especially if the game idea was systems heavy. 

Did this despite knowing the lessons from utilising AI as part of my actual software job, where planning etc leads to better results. 

Managed to squeeze out a 'complete' game but tempted to remake it. Currently building a game that is inspired by the likes of RimWorld and Clanfolk and seeing massive benefits of taking time, planning ahead.

comments.author: lemming1607
comments.body: Do not let ai do QA. Thats your one job. Youre the human, making games for humans. AI cant do that

comments.author: _Fauxpaw
comments.body:
1 feels wrong to me.

I feel it should be: Craft the idea > rough, throwaway prototype > design a gameplay slice thoroughly > build > decide if it's worth extrapolating into a larger project.

comments.author: Comet7777
comments.body: I doubt most games have the full game planned before they start. The actual gameplay and novelty you’re creating is going to dictate changes as you play test.

comments.author: SushiMasterPro
comments.body:
If you start I would advise you to not follow the 1st rule. Just start and learn. Making too big plans can make you stuck or demotivate you.

Thanks for sharing and good luck!

comments.body: mind share how to do the QA lane?

comments.author: TopIntelligent8802
comments.body: lol even naughty dog made a trailer for last of us 2 and only then built a game around the trailer. No one plans everything upfront especially because everything changes

comments.author: Reckonerxy
comments.body:
I actually disagree with your first point, planning an entire game without having a simple protytpe first will only make your first version either too bloated or might take a wrong design turn that im practice would not work. We always tend to overscope on the planning stages and then cut back.

It much better to start with something small and then gradually polish it and add more features as you play your game or get feedback from other, ai made or not.

comments.author: Agile_Branch_8743
comments.body: If it's your first game, the most important advice (using AI or not) is to limit scope: do something small and focus, that allows you to go from a prototype to a finished game. Once you finish your first project, you can go for a bigger one. Then rinse and repeat.

comments.author: distilled-games
comments.body: Thank you for your advice. One thing I would add to your first point: iterate on your idea - alot. And let the AI create mockups. Visualizing my ideas helped me alot to figure out mechanics and how things should work.

comments.author: seele1986
comments.body:
I have found that over planning with AI does nothing but slow you down.  Slam the new feature in and iterate off of it, instead of planning the feature out to a meticulous detail.  Couple rounds of chatting and testing in a sandbox?  Sure.  Beyond that, just put the feature in the game, no matter how janky.  AI is better at quickly pivoting, addressing, and fixing things with CLI/MCP.  So it doesn’t have to be perfect.

I recently added some unique liquid physics to my game.  Quickly tested, and then added it.  AI wanted to spend days planning and thinking about every possible detail.  To hell with that!

comments.author: rb-cloud
comments.body: Waste is part of the creative process. You have to explore, you have to throw things away. You don’t just happen upon the right idea and make something good.
